extracted.intended_audience: fans and practitioners of British comedy panel shows (viewers, producers, researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and descriptive standards for producing and evaluating QI-style British comedy panel quiz episodes, covering scoring, rounds, research, production, and audience/ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring — rewarding 'interestingness'
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the show's creators expected that hardly anyone would be able to give a correct answer without significant prompting, they instead encourage sheer 'interestingness', which is how points are mainly scored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points awarded for interesting answers regardless of correctness; tangential discussions, trains of thought and humorous anecdotes are encouraged. The host or QI researchers ('The QI Elves') normally decide the number of points to give.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeits — penalty for 'obvious but wrong' answers
rubrics_metrics.description: Points are deducted for 'answers which are not only wrong, but pathetically obvious' — typically answers that are generally believed to be true but in fact are misconceptions. These answers, referred to as 'forfeits', are usually indicated by a loud klaxon and alarm bell, flashing lights, and the incorrect answer being flashed on the video screens behind the panellists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forfeits are a clear negative-scoring mechanic; examples include a 10-point deduction for suggesting 'oxygen' as the main ingredient of air. Forfeits tend to be widely believed misconceptions rather than mere wrong guesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring discretion and opacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of points given and taken away are normally decided by the host or beforehand by QI researchers known as 'The QI Elves'. Fry has said, 'I think we all agree that nobody in this universe understands QI's scoring system.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring is intentionally informal and discretionary; negative scores are common and totals may be negative. There is someone paid to check scores and guests are allowed the right of appeal if they believe their score is wrong (though rarely exercised).

rubrics_metrics.name: Buzzers and theme-consistent sound design
rubrics_metrics.description: Panellists are given buzzers to use in signalling a response... From Series D onward, all four sounds are based on the particular episode's theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buzzers are demonstrated at the start and often shortened for repeated use; they can be integral to tasks (e.g., guess the sound) and occasionally influence scoring (points deducted if a buzzer does not match the theme or activates the Klaxon). The regular panellist often receives a 'demeaning' buzzer sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Ignorance final round
rubrics_metrics.description: In a parody of ubiquitous general knowledge quizzes, the final round is off-topic and called 'General Ignorance'. It focuses on seemingly easy questions which have widely believed but wrong answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buzzer usage is enforced in this round ('fingers on buzzers'), and because of the 'obvious but wrong' nature of questions, panellists often incur the greatest point losses. The round's frequency has varied across series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tasks, recurring motifs and thematic dressing
rubrics_metrics.description: In a number of episodes, either the set, the panellists' clothing, the opening theme, or a mixture of all, are changed to match the episode's theme. An extra task may be given during an episode which can earn extra points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include drawing contests, spotting an item on the video screens, waving a 'joker' card, and recurring series-long tasks ('The Elephant in the Room', 'Nobody Knows', 'Spend a Penny'). The host may also perform scientific experiments ('Jolly Japes', 'Knick-Knakes', 'Lab Larks'), with replays shown if the outcome is too fast to be seen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series and episode theming by letter
rubrics_metrics.description: Series of QI are assigned letters in sequence and episodes are themed around topics starting with that letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Series D onward often focused every episode on a single topic beginning with the series letter; episode titles and many production/design decisions tie to the theme. Christmas specials are exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research standards — 'QI Elves' and fact-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: The research for the show is mostly carried out by seven people called the 'QI Elves'. The 'elves' devise the questions for the show, and one is on set during filming who is able to communicate with the host during the show to provide and correct information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research uses sources such as Encyclopædia Britannica and Wikipedia. Approximately 20% of researched material is used in an episode; other material may be used in XL versions, books, or online. There is an established workflow for correcting factual errors later (DVD retractions, blog posts, QI Qibbles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Question secrecy and preparation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The makers of the show insist that the answers are not given to the panellists beforehand. The host is given a list of questions about an hour before the show, for preparatory purposes, but the guests are forbidden to ask for preparatory materials or other help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guests are expected not to prepare; warm-up questions may be provided in rehearsals but panellist preparation is discouraged and viewed negatively if it occurs (there have been controversies about guests who prepare).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording, editing and usable material ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Recordings usually take place over a few weeks; three episodes are typically filmed per week... Roughly 16 questions are asked and about half of those make it into the show; about 20% of material researched is used in a QI episode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filming sessions last up to two hours to produce 30-minute episodes (45 minutes for XL); extensive editing selects highlights, out-takes and experiments for different releases (broadcast, XL, books, web).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction and refunding for factual errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Many factual errors in the show have been corrected in later episodes or on the show's blog. Points were refunded to panellists who had previously been awarded or docked points based on information later shown to be incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers publicly correct errors (DVD features, blogs). Example: points refunded to three panellists, largest refund to Davies (>700 wrongly deducted points). The show maintains mechanisms to receive corrections from the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience participation and scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Points may be given to (or taken from) the studio audience, and six episodes have the distinction of being won by the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience involvement can include tasks, on-screen contributions and even wins; audience forfeits are possible (e.g., −100 for singing German anthem incorrectly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of images and international copyright constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: QI features several images during each episode; there are copyright issues. The pictures in the background of the show are only cleared for UK usage, so until rights are cleared for other territories the programme is unaffordable by smaller countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multimedia licensing affects distribution and format decisions for international sales; producers must clear image rights per territory or limit usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to offensive content and editorial compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Several incidents where jokes caused complaints (e.g., jokes about Tsutomu Yamaguchi; a limerick about paedophilia) led to formal complaints and, in some cases, BBC apologies or decisions to postpone/cancel filming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers must weigh humour against potential offence and adhere to broadcaster guidelines (BBC responses have included apologies and programme scheduling changes). Controversial material may be judged 'capable of causing offence' even if not ruled in breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender representation in panellist selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The BBC has received criticism regarding the lack of women on their comedy panel shows; as a result the corporation decided to ban all-male panels on comedy shows in February 2014.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers and hosts are expected to consider gender balance when booking; statistics on female guest representation are monitored and discussed publicly; host changes have been framed as opportunities to increase female participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host and regular panellist role definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The panel consists of four participants: three rotating guests and one regular, Alan Davies, who has the seat to the immediate right of the host. The host (originally Stephen Fry, later Sandi Toksvig) presents and adjudicates scoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format relies on the host to guide discourse, award/deduct points and maintain tone; the regular panellist provides continuity and is often the foil for forfeits and demeaning introductions as part of the show's style.
